title: Painting at the court
hookLine: Sikh and hill painters made portraits of the court and the Gurus

lines: A PLAIN KING AMONG BRIGHT TURBANS.
cards: A small painting of the kind made for the Lahore court. An old man sits on a cushion in plain clothes, with a white beard, and nothing about him shouts that he's the king.

Around him stand courtiers in bright turbans, in reds and golds and greens. No camera ever caught Ranjit Singh. What we have instead is paint, laid on by hand with fine brushes, by artists who worked for his court.

teach.h: PAINTERS FROM THE HILLS AND THE PUNJAB.
teach.b: Some painters came down from the hill kingdoms north of the Punjab plains, places like Guler and Kangra, with a tradition of small, careful paintings in bright color.
As those hill states came under Lahore's power, painters found new patrons at the Sikh court and among its nobles, and Sikh artists painted alongside them.
They painted the court: portraits of the Maharaja, his sons and ministers, generals on horseback, courtiers in a row, and sometimes the Maharaja himself, plainly dressed among a richly dressed court.
They painted the Gurus too, among them Guru Nanak with his companions Bhai Bala and Bhai Mardana, Mardana with his rabab. These were never likenesses.
No painter of that time had ever seen the Gurus; they were imagining, with devotion, faces they knew only from stories and hymns. Sikhs today hold different views on such pictures.
Some hang them in homes with love; some say the Guru is the Word, not a face, and a picture should never become an object of worship. The Sikh code of conduct rejects the worship of images.
Still, these paintings are one way later generations can see that court: its colors, its clothes, its faces. A kingdom remembered in paint.

how: Sikh paintings from the Lahore court era are kept in museums and collections, and some Sikh homes display later pictures of the Gurus; the Sikh code of conduct rejects the worship of images.

practice: If you can, find a Sikh painting, in a book, on a museum's website or on someone's wall; if not, call one up in your mind.
Look slowly, faces first, then hands, then colors, then edges, and notice one detail you'd normally miss, a fold of cloth, a bird, the shape of a turban. Ask what the painter wanted you to see.
